description: US medical practices assemble payer-specific documentation and track prior-authorization decisions across channels. CMS documents a limited non-drug payer-rule scope; AMA surveys describe a broader medication/procedure authorization workload. Both support administrative workflow research, but the AMA averages cannot be attributed to small practices or to the CMS-covered non-drug subset.
customer_segment: US physician practices and administrative staff. Small independent practices are a hypothesized segment; surveys do not establish their burden distribution. CMS requirements have narrower payer and non-drug scope than the AMA surveys.
geography: United States; payer scope and drug exclusions matter.
context: Administrative work before medical items, services or medications. Keep broad AMA survey figures distinct from the CMS non-drug regulatory subset; no patient information was collected.

evidence.text: CMS describes its rule as reducing prior-authorization burden and specifies APIs for covered items/services, documentation requirements, requests and responses.
The fact sheet specifies denial reasons and describes decision timeframes with payer exclusions.
Practices completed an average of 39 prior authorization requests per physician per week (AMA 2024 survey, n=1,000).
Those requests consumed an average of 13 hours of physician and staff time per physician per week.
The burden persisted a year later: about 40 requests and about 13 hours per week in the AMA 2025 survey, and 40% of physicians employ staff dedicated solely to prior authorization.
82% of physicians in the 2024 survey reported patients abandoned treatment due to prior authorization issues, and more than one in four reported a serious adverse event for a patient in their care.

An earlier AMA survey (web-based, 1,000 physicians, December 2016) reported an average of 37 PA requests per physician per week and 16.4 hours per week of physician and staff time; about one-third of physicians had staff working exclusively on PA, and fax and telephone were the most commonly reported ways to complete requests.

alternatives: Existing payer channels and practice workflows; CMS explicitly discusses portal, fax, email, mail and phone for denial communication.
Payer APIs described by CMS; EHR/vendor adoption and real availability were not tested.
Dedicated prior-authorization staff (used by 40% of physicians per the 2025 survey)
Payer portals and phone/fax follow-up (status quo)
Insurer 'gold card' exemption programs (reported by only 5% of physicians)

contradictory_evidence.text: CMS describes operational requirements generally starting in 2026 and API requirements generally starting in 2027: public infrastructure and incumbent adoption may reduce a new entrant's differentiation.
The rule described excludes drugs and does not cover every US payer; a universal workflow claim would overreach.

Insurers pledged in 2025 to streamline prior authorization and electronic prior-authorization rules are advancing, which could shrink this problem; however only one in three physicians expects meaningful change, and the 2025 measured burden is unchanged.

Prior authorization exists to control inappropriate utilization, and 32% of physicians say requests are often or always denied — some share of the work is the system functioning as designed rather than pure waste. The problem claim is about process cost, not about eliminating review.

The 2016 and 2024/2025 AMA surveys are separate samples from the same advocacy organization, so they show the burden persisting over about nine years but are not independent corroboration from a different source. The 2016 figure (16.4 hours) is higher than the 2024/2025 figure (about 13 hours), so the reported burden has not clearly grown; differences in sample and wording prevent a trend claim.

The earlier AMA surveys and different AMA articles remain evidence from one advocacy organization. They are not independent source corroboration and do not establish willingness to buy an external solution.

uncertainty: No small-practice interviews, independently measured staff time, payer implementation verification or willingness-to-pay evidence. AMA figures are physician self-report, not a time-motion study; dedicated staff demonstrate labor allocation, not demand for a new product. Practice-size distribution, clinical privacy/integration cost and current regulatory implementation remain unknown.
open_questions: Which documentation/response-tracking gaps remain after current EHR and payer integrations in a narrowly defined specialty?
What later changes affect the 2024 rule and actual 2026/2027 implementation?
How is prior-authorization time distributed in small (1-5 physician) practices: who does it, in which tools, and how much is eligibility/status-chasing versus clinical documentation?
What does denial rework add on top of initial submission time?
Which specialties and payer mixes carry the worst load?
Does dental prior authorization (different payer systems) show the same pattern?
next_actions: Check current CMS updates and representative payer/EHR public implementation documentation before any technical opportunity assessment.
Find independent first-hand small-practice evidence; do not treat regulatory intent as a quantified pain estimate.
Investigate the small-practice distribution question above, starting from the full AMA survey data and MGMA sources.
Look for payer-side or CMS data that corroborates volumes independently of the AMA.
title: Prior-authorization requirements and response tracking in medical practices
